question: What does removing a direction r̂ from an activation x leave behind, geometrically?
claim: Projecting x onto a unit direction r̂ splits it into (r̂ᵀx) r̂ along r̂ and a remainder orthogonal to r̂; removing the direction keeps only the remainder.
form: annotated geometry at 1:1 with the direction as the horizontal axis

nodes.label: r̂
nodes.note: drawn 10u below its projection so its tip reads as a vector

edges.note: dotted component lines closing the rectangle, no arrowheads

hue_map.magenta: the unit direction r̂ and every vector that lies along it

forbidden_edges.why: the remainder has no component along r̂; nothing may suggest an angle other than 90 degrees

canvas: the example values in the equations
caption: that the example is 2D and the same decomposition holds in d dimensions
the removal operation x ← x − (r̂ᵀx) r̂ as used for directional ablation

Projecting x onto a unit direction r̂ splits it into (r̂ᵀx) r̂ along r̂ and a remainder orthogonal to r̂; removing the direction keeps only the remainder. Magenta marks r̂ and everything that lies along it; dotted lines are the components that close the rectangle. Drawn to scale for x = (3, 2) and r̂ = (1, 0); in d dimensions the remainder lies in the (d − 1)-dimensional complement r̂⊥.
